title: Wherever Rama's story is told
hook: Hanuman finds a way to reach a frightened Sita: he tells her Rama's story
carry: where rama's story is told, hanuman listens

segments.voice: Yesterday: a blade of grass between Sita and Ravana, and your line: Sita and Ram, never apart, like light and sun.

Ravana has gone. The guards have finished threatening her and drawn back. Sita sits alone at the foot of the tree, worn out, close to the end of hope. Hanuman is right above her. He has found her, and now he faces a delicate problem. A monkey suddenly dropping out of a tree and talking, in the middle of the enemy's garden, could terrify her. If she cries out, the guards wake, and everything is lost.
screen: `SITA, ALONE, NEAR THE END OF HOPE.` → `HANUMAN, RIGHT ABOVE HER.` → `ONE CRY AND IT'S LOST.`

segments.voice: So once again Valmiki lets us hear Hanuman think. If I speak polished Sanskrit, like a learned priest, she'll think I'm Ravana in disguise; Ravana fooled her once already, dressed as a holy man. So I'll use plain, everyday speech. And I won't start with myself. I'll start with Rama. Softly, from the branches, he begins to tell a story, as if to no one. There was a king called Dasharatha, righteous and great. His eldest son Rama was sent into the forest with his wife and his brother. In the forest, his wife Sita was carried off. Rama searched for her, made friends with the monkey king Sugriva, and sent monkeys everywhere to find her. And I crossed the ocean, and I have seen her. That's all. The first thing she hears is her husband's name, and Sita lifts her head. Notice what Hanuman is doing up there: telling Rama's story to someone in sorrow. Hindus have done it ever since. Families read the Ramayana aloud in hard times, and a Sundara Kanda path, a reading of this very book, is a common way to pray. And there's a loved belief about who is listening. A verse many recite before a reading says: wherever Rama's glory is sung, Hanuman is there, palms joined above his head, eyes full of tears. So at many readings a seat is kept empty for him. Hanuman was the first to tell Rama's story in Lanka. Hindus believe he never stopped listening.
screen: `PLAIN WORDS, NOT PRIESTLY SANSKRIT.` · `RAMA'S STORY, TOLD SOFTLY.` · `SITA LIFTS HER HEAD.` · then, large: `WHEREVER IT'S SUNG, HANUMAN IS THERE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, tell Rama's story to yourself in three plain sentences, the way Hanuman told it in the tree: a prince sent to the forest, his wife carried off, a friend who crossed the sea to find her. Some people leave a little space beside them as they do, for the listener Hindus believe comes. If you don't pray, bring to mind a story that once steadied you, and tell it to yourself softly, start to finish, breathing slowly.
Sita found. Hanuman, above her in the tree, tells Rama's story softly in plain words, so the first thing Sita hears is the name she loves.
Your line: where Rama's story is told, Hanuman listens. That's why some readings keep a seat for him. Day six hundred eighteen, done.
